title: What is a stock?
subtitle: A certificate of ownership in part of a business
openingQuestion: When you buy 100 shares of a listed company, what are you actually doing?
openingOptions: Lending the company money to earn interest
Buying one of the company's products
Betting on the price going up or down, much like a casino game
Becoming a part-owner, with rights to profit and assets
explanation: A stock (or share) is a certificate of ownership in part of a business. A shareholder has the right to: receive dividends (if the company distributes them), vote at the shareholder meeting, and receive a share of the remaining assets if the company is dissolved (after all debts are paid). This is completely different from a bond - a shareholder is an owner, not a creditor.

diagram.label: An investor buys → becomes a shareholder

realWorldExample.description: When you buy VNM (Vinamilk) shares on the HOSE exchange, you own an extremely tiny but real slice of the company - including its factories, its brand, and the right to receive dividends proportional to your ownership.

quiz.question: What happens to shareholders if a company goes bankrupt and has to liquidate its assets?
options: They get their original contributed capital back ahead of other creditors
They receive whatever remains after every creditor has been paid
They're paid on equal footing alongside bondholders
They're refunded a percentage based on the shares they hold
quiz.explanation: The payout priority order in bankruptcy is: secured creditors → unsecured creditors (including bondholders) → preferred shareholders → common shareholders, paid last. This is why stocks carry higher risk than bonds but, in exchange, also higher potential return.

quiz.question: If a company issues additional preferred stock that has the right to a fixed dividend ahead of common shareholders, how does this affect the risk position of existing common shareholders?
options: Unchanged, since preferred stock is still equity
Risk falls, because the company raises new capital
Risk rises, because there's now an extra layer paid ahead of them
Unchanged, because preferred dividends are paid after tax
quiz.explanation: Preferred stock sits between bonds and common stock in the priority order - it has the right to a fixed dividend and liquidation priority ahead of common shareholders but behind creditors, which leaves common shareholders always in the riskiest position in the capital structure.

quiz.question: What are the three basic rights of a common shareholder?
options: Buying more shares at cost, voting, and being exempt from tax
Receiving fixed interest, voting, and withdrawing capital anytime
Receiving dividends, priority debt repayment, and appointing the director
Receiving dividends, voting, and a share of remaining assets
quiz.explanation: A common shareholder has the right to receive dividends if the company decides to distribute them, vote at the shareholder meeting, and receive a share of what remains upon dissolution. None of those rights is guaranteed - quite unlike bond interest.

quiz.question: Why is a stock riskier than a bond of the same business?
options: Because shareholders get paid last, with nothing guaranteed
Because a stock generally has a shorter holding period than a bond
Because stock prices move every session while bond prices don't
Because dividends are taxed while bond interest is exempt
quiz.explanation: A bondholder has a contract requiring interest and principal to be paid; a shareholder only receives whatever is left. In bankruptcy, what's left is usually nothing - which is why shareholders demand a higher expected return.

quiz.question: Where does preferred stock sit in the payout priority order?
options: Ahead of even secured creditors
Behind creditors but ahead of common shareholders
On equal footing with unsecured bonds
Behind common shareholders since preferred dividends are fixed
quiz.explanation: Preferred stock is the layer in between: a fixed dividend and priority ahead of common shareholders, but still ranked behind every debt obligation. That's why it's seen as a hybrid between debt and equity.

keyTakeaways: A stock: a certificate of ownership in part of a business
Shareholders have the right to receive dividends, vote, and share in remaining assets upon dissolution
Higher risk than bonds because they're paid last if the company goes bankrupt

practicePrompt.question: A friend says: 'Buying Vinamilk stock is just like lending Vinamilk money, and they'll pay you back with interest.' Does this correctly capture the nature of owning a stock?
options: Correct, buying stock is essentially identical to lending a company money and receiving periodic interest like a bond
Wrong - a share is a claim of part-ownership in the business, not a loan you have made to it
Partly correct, because a stock is both an ownership right and a loan with a fixed interest rate
Incorrect, because a stock is just a piece of paper with no real economic value at all
practicePrompt.explanation: A stock: a certificate of ownership in part of a business - completely different from a bond (a loan with a fixed interest rate and term). A shareholder shares both the risk (of losing capital) and the profit (unlimited) with the company, with no repayment commitment like a creditor has.

summary.keyIdea: A stock: a certificate of ownership in part of a business
summary.commonMistake: Reading the concept as a phrase to memorize rather than a principle to apply to a real decision.
summary.action: Shareholders have the right to receive dividends, vote, and share in remaining assets upon dissolution

application.title: Check the stock you're holding
application.message: If you already own some stock, look up whether that company pays dividends and what voting rights you actually have at the shareholder meeting - that's the real benefit you're holding.
application.secondary: Many people buy stock without ever noticing what rights they actually hold.

sections.text: A stock isn't just a number flickering on a screen - it's a certificate that you own a real slice of a real business, with its own factories, brand, staff, and cash flow. Buying a VNM share means you become a co-owner of Vinamilk, however small the ratio.
Three benefits that come with a stock

A shareholder has three basic rights: (1) receive dividends if the company decides to distribute them; (2) vote at the shareholder meeting on major matters such as electing the board, mergers, issuing new shares; (3) receive a share of the remaining assets if the company is dissolved - but only after everything owed to creditors has been paid. These three rights are exactly what creates the real economic value behind that stock certificate.
Why shareholders carry more risk than bondholders

When a company goes bankrupt, the repayment order is always: secured creditors → unsecured creditors (including bondholders) → preferred shareholders → common shareholders. Common shareholders stand at the back of the line - if the liquidated assets aren't enough to cover all the debt, shareholders lose everything. This is why stock is always considered a riskier asset than bonds, and in exchange, has far greater profit potential if the business succeeds.

items: Dividends aren't a mandatory obligation like bond interest - the company can withhold them at any time
Preferred stock sits between bondholders and common shareholders in the priority order
Voting rights are proportional to the number of shares held, not by headcount
Common shareholders are always the group bearing the highest risk in the entire capital structure

lines: Owning a stock is owning risk and opportunity at the same time - understanding your position in the capital structure is the first step toward disciplined investing.
